title: Whiplash-Associated Disorders (WAD)

differentials.name: Cervical fracture or instability
differentials.key: High-risk mechanism, midline tenderness, severe pain, neurological signs

differentials.name: Cervical radiculopathy
differentials.key: Arm pain in a root pattern, neurological deficit

differentials.name: Concussion
differentials.key: Head impact, confusion, memory loss, headache, nausea

differentials.name: Cervical artery dissection
differentials.key: Unusual severe neck or head pain, neurological symptoms (the 5 Ds, Section G)

differentials.name: Vestibular disorder
differentials.key: Spinning vertigo with head position change

qa: Does she need imaging under the Canadian C-spine rule? No. No high-risk factor; low-risk factors present; she can rotate 45 degrees each way.
Why avoid a soft collar? Immobilisation is associated with slower recovery; active movement is preferred.
What would change her grade to III? Neurological signs such as reduced reflexes, weakness or sensory loss.
Which factors would make you worry about a slow recovery? High pain intensity, high NDI, post-traumatic stress symptoms and widespread sensitivity.
She becomes dizzy with double vision during treatment. What do you do? Stop immediately, treat as a possible vascular event and arrange emergency care.

fields.Purpose: Assess deep neck flexor control and endurance
fields.Patient position: Crook lying, head in neutral, pressure biofeedback unit placed under the neck and inflated to 20 mmHg
fields.Therapist position: Beside the head, watching the dial and the superficial neck muscles
fields.Action: Patient performs a gentle head nod (as if saying "yes") to raise the pressure in 2 mmHg stages from 22 to 30 mmHg, holding each stage for 10 seconds
fields.Positive (impaired): Unable to reach or hold stages, uses superficial muscles (sternocleidomastoid), jaw clenching, chin poking
fields.Interpretation: Impaired motor control, a treatment target, not a diagnosis
fields.Next step: Start training at the highest stage held well

fields.Purpose: Assess cervical proprioception in dizzy patients
fields.Position: Sitting 90 cm from a wall target, laser on headband, eyes closed
fields.Action: Patient turns the head to one side and returns to the "start" position; measure distance from the centre
fields.Positive: Consistent errors larger than expected [Ref – to verify threshold]

redFlags.Finding: Midline bony tenderness, high-risk mechanism, age 65 or over, limb paraesthesia after trauma
redFlags.Immediate action: Immobilise; do not move the neck; imaging

redFlags.Finding: Bilateral limb symptoms, gait disturbance, bladder change
Dizziness, diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, drop attacks, nystagmus, numbness of the face
Loss of consciousness, worsening headache, repeated vomiting, confusion

manual.name: Gentle cervical and thoracic mobilisation (Maitland grades I to II early, III later)
manual.why: Short-term pain relief and confidence in movement
manual.finding: Painful, limited segmental movement after fracture is excluded
manual.application: Supine or sitting; small rhythmic oscillations within comfort

manual.name: Thoracic manipulation
manual.why: Short-term relief of neck pain [Ref – to verify]
manual.application: Supine or sitting thrust after consent

manualNotes: Preferred starting choice: education plus active exercise. Manual therapy is an adjunct, not the main treatment. Avoid passive-only care that teaches the patient to depend on the therapist.

exercise.Steps: Slow rotation, side flexion, flexion, extension within comfort
Supine nod, pressure biofeedback at the stage held well
Band rows with shoulder blades drawn back and down

exercise.Exercise: Gaze stability and JPE training (if dizzy)
exercise.Steps: Relocate head to target with eyes closed; keep eyes on target while turning head

exerciseNotes: Symptom rule: mild increase during exercise that settles within a few hours is acceptable.

modalities.name: Soft collar
modalities.comment: Prolonged immobilisation delays recovery [Ref – to verify]

modalities.name: Ultrasound, laser
modalities.comment: No meaningful benefit shown [Ref – to verify]

pathway: Acute (0 to 2 weeks): exclude fracture and serious injury; reassure; "stay active, move within comfort"; simple exercises; advise about analgesia through the doctor.
Subacute (2 to 12 weeks): progressive exercise, motor control, sensorimotor training, gradual return to driving and work.
Persistent (over 12 weeks): combine exercise with pain education, sleep and stress management; refer for psychological care if post-traumatic stress features are present.
